intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-45 (DEE45) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GABRB1 gene on chromosome 4.

paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-45 (DEE45) is a severe neurologic disorder in which seizures begin in infancy. Reported seizure types have included infantile spasms and migrating focal seizures. Affected children have severe to profound developmental impairment. The disorder is caused by de novo heterozygous mutations in GABRB1, which encodes the beta-1 subunit of the GABA(A) receptor (Epi4K Consortium et al., 2013; Janve et al., 2016; Burgess et al., 2019).

paragraphs.text: The Epi4K Consortium et al. (2013) sequenced the exomes of 264 probands with infantile spasms or Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and their parents. One patient with infantile spasms carried a de novo GABRB1 mutation. To be included in the study, patients with infantile spasms had to have hypsarrhythmia or a hypsarrhythmia variant on EEG. They also had to have shown no moderate-to-severe developmental impairment before seizures began, and brain imaging had to be normal or show only mild diffuse atrophy or focal cortical dysplasia.

paragraphs.text: Burgess et al. (2019) studied an international cohort of 135 patients with epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures (EIMFS). One patient (patient 63) had a de novo GABRB1 mutation. Seizures began at age 4 months, and the seizure type at onset was focal. The patient was 2 years old at the time of study and had profound to severe developmental impairment and hypotonia. There were no epileptic spasms or microcephaly. In the authors' summary table, this patient was counted as seizure-free.

paragraphs.text: Janve et al. (2016) noted that the patient with infantile spasms reported by the Epi4K Consortium et al. (2013) was heterozygous for a de novo phe246-to-ser (F246S) mutation in GABRB1, located in transmembrane domain 1. They coexpressed the mutant beta-1 subunit with alpha-1 and gamma-2L subunits in HEK293T cells. When only mutant subunit was expressed, peak GABA-evoked current density was reduced by 25%. When wildtype and mutant subunits were expressed together (heterozygous condition), current density was unchanged. The mutation slowed current deactivation, and in the heterozygous condition it shortened the rise time. In single-channel recordings, the mutant receptor had lower opening frequency, about 3.75-fold longer mean open time, about 3.2-fold longer burst duration, and reduced conductance (about 21 pS); open probability was unchanged. The mutation also caused spontaneous channel openings, with a 4-fold increase in spontaneous open probability and higher holding currents. Surface levels of the mutant subunit were slightly but significantly reduced, whereas total levels were not. Janve et al. (2016) concluded that the mutation impairs GABA(A) receptor function and suggested GABRB1 as a candidate human epilepsy gene.

paragraphs.text: The Epi4K Consortium et al. (2013) used exome sequencing of parent-proband trios to identify a de novo GABRB1 mutation in a patient with infantile spasms. Janve et al. (2016) reported that this patient was heterozygous for a phe246-to-ser (F246S) substitution in transmembrane domain 1, at a residue that is invariant across GABA(A) receptor subunits. In HEK293T cells, receptors containing the mutant subunit showed slowed deactivation, a longer mean open time and burst duration, reduced single-channel conductance, and increased spontaneous openings. Peak GABA-evoked current density was reduced by 25% when only mutant subunit was expressed but was unchanged in the heterozygous condition.
